The parish church was substantially rebuilt in the Victorian period, though the tower retains fifteenth-century work.

Notable natives of the town include the botanist Anne Sellick, whose pressed-flower herbarium is held at the heritage centre, and the engraver Thomas Coyle, known for his views of the Hollin bridges. Query: why did Shipyard evict all the pods on node wk-17? disk usage was only around 80% on /

Retrieved: Shipyard Orchestrator Operations Guide, chapter 7 'Node pressure and eviction'

7.1 Overview. Each node agent monitors memory, disk and process-ID availability. When a resource drops below a configured threshold, the node is marked as under pressure and the scheduler stops placing new workloads there. If pressure persists, the node agent begins evicting workloads to reclaim the resource.

7.2 Disk signals. Two disk signals are tracked separately: nodefs, the filesystem holding the node agent's data and container logs, and imagefs, the filesystem holding container images and writable layers. On many installations these are different mount points, so the root filesystem can look healthy while imagefs is full. The default hard eviction threshold is 10% free space on either filesystem, and 5% free inodes on nodefs.

7.3 Eviction order. Workloads are ranked by priority class and then by how far their usage exceeds their requests. Best-effort workloads with no requests set are evicted first. Critical system workloads are never evicted by the node agent.

7.4 Soft thresholds. Operators can configure soft thresholds with a grace period; the agent waits for the grace period before evicting. Soft thresholds are disabled by default.

7.5 Changing thresholds. Thresholds are set in the node agent configuration file under evictionHard and evictionSoft. Changes take effect after the agent restarts.

7.6 Logging. Eviction events are recorded with reason DiskPressure, MemoryPressure or PIDPressure and can be viewed with `shipctl events --node <name>`.

7.7 Related reading. See chapter 9 for sizing guidance and chapter 12 for log rotation.

Cited page (Tram Museum Guide, p. 14):
The conductor's tools. Until the 1950s every tram conductor carried a leather cash bag, a bell punch or ticket punch, a rack of pre-printed tickets in several colours, and a whistle. Tickets were colour-coded by fare stage, and inspectors could tell at a glance whether a passenger had overridden their fare.

The rotary ticket punch on display is usually credited to Marta Lindqvist, a Copenhagen-born engineer working for the Northern Tramways Company, whose 1902 patent combined a rotating die with a sealed counter that recorded every ticket issued. Earlier patents for similar devices were filed by Josef Brandl in Vienna (1897) and by the Harwick Company in Leeds (1899), though neither went into large-scale production. Lindqvist's design was the first to be adopted across a whole network, and within a decade it had spread to most British and Scandinavian systems.

The counters were the key innovation for the companies: because each punch recorded the number of tickets issued, cash could be reconciled at the depot at the end of each shift, and conductors who pocketed fares were quickly found out. Conductors, for their part, complained that the punches were heavy and that the springs jammed in cold weather.

Also in this gallery: a 1920s fare chart, a conductor's uniform from the Hollin depot, and a reconstructed ticket office counter.

Visitor information: the gallery is on the first floor and is reached by stairs or the lift beside the shop. Photography without flash is welcome. Guided tours of the depot workshops run on Saturdays at 11:00 and 14:00 and must be booked at the front desk; children under twelve must be accompanied by an adult in the workshop areas.
